newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA POLICE STEPS UP FIGHT AGAINST CORRUPTION.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA POLICE STEPS UP FIGHT AGAINST CORRUPTION.

text.p: Bulgarian police said on Monday it had started checks on firms operating in Bulgaria's Black Sea resorts, stepping up a fight against corruption and organised crime.
A ministry statement said hotels, restaurants, night clubs, shops and gambling houses had been checked in the three biggest resorts situated in the country's northern sea-side.

"A joint investigation started today in the resorts in the northern sea-side involving officials from the ministries of interior, environment, finance, health, trade and tourism and the National Pricing Committee," it said.

"The most typical violations included a lack of documents for giving premises for rent, price lists and cash machines, licences for alcohol sales and unlabeled bottles with alcohol offered for sale" the statement said.
In Bulgaria bottles with alcohol and packages with cigarettes must be offered with labels proving that their excise duty has been paid.
Checks in all Black Sea resorts will continue, the statement said.

Police have also started unexpected investigation over the weekend on the property of some 1,000 customs officers at 49 border check-points aimed at cracking down on ill-gotten gains, another ministry statement said.

Police, checking whether their vehicles, land, houses and hard currency were lawfully owned, said that "a big part of the customs officers have modern and new limousines and live in luxurious conditions".
A customs officer suspected in corruption has been detained, as well as a vehicle whose engine and car body numbers have been scraped off and new ones have been engraved.
Officials say the traffic of stolen cars through Bulgaria is huge, many vehicles being re-exported to Moldova, Ukraine and other ex-Soviet republics or Macedonia, Albania, and Yugoslavia.

Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev, who retained his post from the interim government which took office in February, has vowed to stem the crime and corruption which have flourished in the seven years since the end of one-party rule.
Bonev's ministry first step was a high-profile check on luxury cars dubbed Operation Mosquito, to crack down on car theft and tax evasion in March.
The ministry said some 14,600 cars were inspected around the country, and 100 were found to have altered serial numbers, suggesting they had been stolen.

Bulgaria's new government, which took over two weeks ago, has targeted cracking down on organised crime and corruption as one of its priorities in an attempt to make the country more attractive to potential foreign investors.
